491.title: Forgive and have mercy
491.hook: my Lord, forgive and have mercy, You are the best of the merciful (23:118)
491.howItsDone: Many Muslims memorize 23:118 and repeat it as a short supplication, often counting it on their fingers or prayer beads after the daily prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, clay, drop, clot, bone, flesh, and your line was blessed is the best creator. What part of you did you catch working? Day four hundred ninety-one.

Some books save the best line for the last page. Surah Al-Mu'minun does something like that. It opened, two days ago, with a bright promise: successful are the believers. Near its end, it goes somewhere dark. People who have died call out, my Lord, send me back, so that I might do right in what I left behind. And they're told it's only a word they're saying. Then the surah gathers itself and closes. Its very last verse is a short prayer, handed to the Prophet ﷺ to say. Today, that last line.

Verse one hundred eighteen. Pickthall: "And (O Muhammad) say: My Lord! Forgive and have mercy, for Thou art Best of all who show mercy." In Arabic: rabbi ghfir warham, wa anta khayru r-rahimin. Two verbs, ighfir and irham. Forgive, and have mercy. They aren't the same request. Ghafara has a sense of covering, of putting something over a fault so it no longer stands exposed. Rahma, mercy, is wider. It's the root of ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim in the bismillah, and many scholars connect it to rahim, the womb: care that surrounds you before you've done anything to earn it. So the prayer asks for two things. Cover what I've done wrong. And hold me anyway. Then it gives the reason: You are the best of those who show mercy. Remember Ayyub, nine days ago, calling God the most merciful of the merciful. Different surah, close to the same title. And look where the line sits. Right after the people who begged to be sent back. They asked for a second chance after it was too late. This verse is the version you say while there's still time. And the surah's bookends are worth noticing. It begins, qad aflaha l-mu'minun, successful are the believers. Just before this prayer, it says the deniers will not be successful, la yuflihu. Success at the start, the lack of it near the end, and between them, one short sentence anyone can carry.
screen: `RABBI GHFIR WARHAM.` · `COVER IT, AND HOLD ME ANYWAY.` · `SAID WHILE THERE'S STILL TIME.` · `SUCCESS AT BOTH ENDS OF THE SURAH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say it ten times. Sit, and let the breath settle. If you pray, say the line slowly, ten times, in Arabic or English: my Lord, forgive and have mercy, You are the best of the merciful. Count on your fingers if that helps. If you don't pray, let ten breaths go by, and on each one think of something you'd like covered, and someone you'd like to be held. The bell holds the time.
Rahma. Mercy, wider than forgiveness: the last verse of Al-Mu'minun asks God to cover what's wrong and hold us anyway. Today's word.
Your line: best of the merciful. Today, when someone makes a small mistake near you, try covering it rather than pointing at it. Day four hundred ninety-one.

what it means: two requests, cover my fault and hold me in mercy, with the reason: You are the best of the merciful.
what a scholar hears: the surah's ring: qad aflaha (23:1) and la yuflihu (23:117); khayru r-rahimin here, arhamu r-rahimin in Ayyub's call (21:83).

492.title: Light upon light
492.hook: His light is like a niche with a lamp in glass like a shining star, lit from a blessed olive (24:35)
492.howItsDone: The Verse of Light, 24:35, is often recited and often appears in Islamic calligraphy; some medieval mosque lamps were inscribed with it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rahma, the last line of Al-Mu'minun, and your line was best of the merciful. Whose small mistake did you cover? Day four hundred ninety-two.

Before electricity, a house at night had one or two small lights, and people knew them intimately. A clay lamp with a wick floating in olive oil. A little hollow cut into the wall to set it in, so the draft wouldn't catch it and the plaster would throw the light back into the room. Glass, if you were lucky, to make the flame burn steady and bright. Surah An-Nur, the Light, takes that ordinary object, the lamp in the wall, and uses it to describe something nobody can describe. Today, the Verse of Light.

It begins with a sentence that is almost too large: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth." Then, straight away, it gets small. The likeness of His light is a niche, a mishkat, and in it a lamp. The lamp is in a glass. The glass is like a shining star. The lamp is lit from a blessed tree, an olive, neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil would almost glow on its own, even if no fire touched it. And then the phrase this day is named for: "Light upon light." Notice how the picture is built in layers. A niche holds a lamp. The lamp sits in glass. The glass shines like a star. The oil is nearly light already. Each layer gathers the light and makes it brighter, until the verse simply runs out of images and says it: light on top of light. The verse ends by saying God guides to His light whom He wills, and sets out likenesses for people. It doesn't pretend the picture is the thing itself. It's a likeness, a way in. Commentators have read the layers in many ways: the believer's heart as the niche, the Qur'an as the oil, the Prophet as the lamp. The theologian al-Ghazali wrote a book on this verse, called The Niche of Lights. And the olive neither of the east nor of the west? Some say a tree standing in the open, catching sun all day. Others say it points beyond every direction. The verse leaves it open.
screen: `THE LIGHT OF THE HEAVENS AND EARTH.` · `NICHE, LAMP, GLASS, STAR.` · `OIL THAT ALMOST GLOWS.` · `LIGHT UPON LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light a lamp and look. If you can, switch on a small lamp or light a candle somewhere safe, and turn off the brighter lights around it. If not, look at whatever light is nearest, a window, a screen dimmed low. Watch how it falls on the wall behind it, how the wall gives some of it back. Let the layers add up. If you pray, you can say the verse's opening line quietly. The bell holds the time.
Light upon light. Nurun 'ala nur. The Verse of Light's picture of a niche, a lamp, a glass and an oil that almost shines by itself. Today's word.
Your line: light upon light. Tonight, when the lights come on, notice one lamp, and let it be a niche for a moment. Day four hundred ninety-two.

493.title: Why didn't you think well?
493.hook: when you heard the slander, why didn't believers think good of their own (24:12)
493.howItsDone: Muslim teachers often cite 24:12 and the story of the slander, the ifk, when teaching about rumor and gossip, and encourage husn al-zann, thinking well of others, as an everyday habit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Verse of Light, and your line was light upon light. Which lamp did you notice last night? Day four hundred ninety-three.

An army is on its way home through the desert. At one stop, a young woman steps away from camp, and on the way back finds her necklace is missing. She goes back to look for it. When she returns, the camp is gone. Her litter was loaded onto the camel without anyone noticing she wasn't inside. She waits. A man who traveled behind the army finds her, lets her ride, and leads the camel back on foot. They arrive together, in daylight. And within hours, people are talking. The woman is 'A'isha, the Prophet's wife. Today, the rumor.

Bukhari preserves 'A'isha's own long account. The rumor spread through Medina for about a month. She fell ill and didn't know what was being said until a woman told her. She wept for two nights. Then verses of Surah An-Nur came down, declaring her innocent. And look at the first question those verses ask. Not, why did the slanderers lie? But this, in Pickthall's words: "Why did not the believers, men and women, when ye heard it, think good of their own folk, and say: It is a manifest untruth?" The question is aimed at the listeners. The ordinary people who heard it and passed it on, or just let it sit in their heads. A few verses later the surah describes how it happened: you took it up with your tongues, and spoke with your mouths of what you had no knowledge of, and counted it a small thing, when with God it was great. That's how a rumor travels: it seems small. The word this day carries is husn al-zann: thinking well. Zann is an assumption, a guess about someone you can't fully see. Husn is goodness. So husn al-zann is choosing the good guess. And a hadith in Bukhari gives the other side: beware of suspicion, for suspicion is the most false of talk. The surah doesn't ask people to be naive. It asks them to begin from good faith, especially about their own, and to say plainly when something is unproven. Think well first. The facts can come after.
screen: `'A'ISHA'S OWN ACCOUNT.` · `THE QUESTION IS FOR THE LISTENERS.` · `IT SEEMED SMALL; IT WAS GREAT.` · `HUSN AL-ZANN: CHOOSE THE GOOD GUESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: assume the best of someone. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of one person whose behavior lately has bothered you. A late reply, a cold tone, a decision you didn't understand. Now come up with three generous explanations for it. Not excuses, just possibilities you can't rule out. Hold the kindest one for a while. If you pray, you can ask to think well of them. The bell holds the time.
Husn al-zann. Thinking well: choosing the good assumption about someone when you don't know the whole story. Today's word.
Your line: think well first. Today, when a piece of gossip reaches you, let it stop with you. Day four hundred ninety-three.

494.title: Lower the gaze
494.hook: believing men and women are both told to lower their gaze and guard their modesty (24:30–31)
494.howItsDone: Many Muslims understand lowering the gaze as avoiding lingering or immodest looks, for men and women alike, and some extend it to what they choose to watch online.

segments.voice: Yesterday, husn al-zann, and your line was think well first. Did a rumor reach you, and did it stop with you? Day four hundred ninety-four.

A face across the train carriage. A stranger's phone screen, lit up and readable. A photo that stops the thumb mid-scroll. The eyes move first, before anyone has decided anything, and then they linger. Advertisers know this, and so does every app built to keep a thumb scrolling. Surah An-Nur gives a short instruction about the eyes. It is often remembered as a rule for women alone. Look at who hears it first.

Verse thirty. Pickthall: "Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and be modest." Men first. Then the next verse turns to women with the same opening: "And tell the believing women to lower their gaze and be modest". Same verbs. Same duty. The verse to women continues with more detail about dress, and scholars have written a great deal about that. But the gaze comes first, and it's shared. The Arabic is yaghuddu min absarihim. Ghadd means to lower, to lessen, the way you'd lower your voice. And the little word min, from, matters. Some commentators read it as: lower some of your gaze. Not shut your eyes. Not walk around staring at your shoes. You still see the person you're talking to. What gets lowered is the lingering, the second look that turns into staring. A hadith in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi makes the same point. The Prophet ﷺ told 'Ali: don't follow one glance with another. The first is yours; the second is not. The first look just happens. The second one is a choice. And this isn't only about attraction. In a hadith in Bukhari, the Prophet listed the rights of the road for people who sit by the street, and lowering the gaze is the first of them. Next to it: not harming anyone, returning greetings, encouraging good. So guarding the eyes is also manners. It's not staring at the neighbor's open door, not reading the stranger's messages over their shoulder, not lingering on someone who'd rather not be looked at.
screen: `MEN ADDRESSED FIRST.` · `GHADD: LOWER, LESSEN.` · `THE FIRST LOOK IS YOURS.` · `A RIGHT OF THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: guard your eyes for an hour. Sit, and let the breath settle. Lower your gaze gently toward the floor in front of you. Not closed, just softened. Notice how often your eyes want to move. Each time they do, let them come back. Then decide on one hour today, maybe your commute or a scrolling hour, when you'll keep the first look and let go of the second. The bell holds the time.
Ghadd al-basar. Lowering the gaze: keep the first look, let go of the second. Said first to men, then to women. Today's word.
Your line: guard the eyes. Today, notice one second look you're about to take, on the street or on a screen, and let it go. Day four hundred ninety-four.

what it means: a shared duty, men first, to lower the lingering second look, and part of everyday manners too.

495.title: Knock and greet
495.hook: don't enter houses until you've asked permission and greeted the people (24:27)
495.tomorrow: Don't you want to be forgiven?
495.howItsDone: Muslim families often teach children to knock, say as-salamu 'alaykum and wait before entering a room, following 24:27–28 and the hadith on asking permission three times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ghadd al-basar, lowering the gaze, and your line was guard the eyes. Which second look did you let go? Day four hundred ninety-five.

Commentators on this verse describe an older habit. A visitor would walk straight into a house and call out a greeting once already inside, good morning, to someone who might not be ready to be seen. Sometimes a curtain was all that stood in the way. Surah An-Nur, a surah full of rules about privacy and dignity, sets down a small one about thresholds. It's so ordinary you could miss how much it says. Today, the knock.

Verse twenty-seven. Pickthall begins: "O ye who believe! Enter not houses other than your own". And then: not until you've made yourselves known, and greeted the people inside with peace. The verb for making yourself known is tasta'nisu. Commentators link it to uns, the word for ease, friendliness, feeling at home with someone. So it isn't only asking permission. It's waiting until the people inside are comfortable with you being there. Then the next verse adds: if you find no one at home, don't go in. And if you're told to go back, go back. That is purer for you. No argument, no peering through the window. The hadith fill in the picture. Bukhari records Abu Musa going to 'Umar's house, asking permission three times, getting no answer, and leaving. When 'Umar later asked why he'd left, Abu Musa said the Prophet ﷺ taught: ask permission three times, and if you're not given it, go back. Another report, in Abu Dawud, says that when the Prophet came to someone's door, he would stand to one side of it, not facing straight in, and give the greeting. That's the whole lesson in a posture. Stand where you can't see in. Say peace. Wait. So knock and greet isn't fussy etiquette. It's a picture of respect for another person's space, the part of their life they get to decide about. Today the doors have locks and the houses have bells, but the same idea reaches a bedroom door, a phone left on a table, a message thread that isn't yours.
screen: `ENTER NOT HOUSES NOT YOUR OWN.` · `TASTA'NISU: UNTIL THEY'RE AT EASE.` · `ASK THREE TIMES, THEN GO BACK.` · `STAND TO ONE SIDE OF THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: knock and wait. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of the doors you go through without knocking. A family member's room. A colleague's desk. A friend's phone, a shared screen. Picture yourself standing beside one of them, knocking, and waiting, a few breaths longer than feels natural, until you're welcome. If you pray, you can say the greeting of peace to yourself as you picture it. The bell holds the time.
Uns. Ease, the familiarity a visitor waits for before entering: make yourself known, say peace, and wait until you're welcome. Today's word.
Your line: ask before entering. Today, knock on one door you'd usually walk straight through, and wait for the answer. Day four hundred ninety-five.

496.title: Don't you want to be forgiven?
496.hook: Abu Bakr forgives a relative who spread the slander after this verse: pardon and overlook (24:22)
496.howItsDone: Muslim teachers often tell the story of Abu Bakr and Mistah with 24:22 when speaking about forgiveness within families, and many Muslims recall its question when they find it hard to let go of a grievance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, uns, knock and greet, and your line was ask before entering. Which door did you knock on and wait? Day four hundred ninety-six.

Three days ago we heard the rumor about 'A'isha. Now the other side of it. Her father, Abu Bakr, had a poor relative named Mistah, a cousin's son, and for years Abu Bakr had been paying for his keep. When the slander spread, Mistah was one of the people repeating it. About his own benefactor's daughter. After the verses came down clearing her, Abu Bakr swore an oath: he would never spend on Mistah again. Most of us would call that fair. Then another verse came down.

Verse twenty-two. It speaks to people of means who swear not to give to their relatives, the poor, and those who emigrated for God's sake. Mistah was all three. And then, in Pickthall's words: "Let them forgive and show indulgence. Yearn ye not that Allah may forgive you?" Two verbs again. Ya'fu: to pardon, to let the debt go. Yasfahu: to overlook, to turn away from it, to stop bringing it up. Scholars often describe the second as going one step further than the first: not only letting the wrong go, but not holding it over the person afterward. And then the question. Not a command, a question. Don't you want God to forgive you? 'A'isha's account in Bukhari says that when Abu Bakr heard this, he said: yes, by God, I want God to forgive me. And he went back to supporting Mistah, and said he would never stop. Look at what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say Mistah was right. It doesn't say the harm was small; the verses before called it great. It doesn't ask Abu Bakr to trust Mistah with secrets. It asks him not to cut off the support that kept a poor relative fed. Pardon isn't pretending it didn't happen, and it isn't letting someone keep hurting you. It's refusing to make the rest of the relationship pay for one wound. And the reason it gives is personal. Everyone needs forgiving for something.
screen: `AN OATH TO STOP GIVING.` · `PARDON, AND OVERLOOK.` · `DON'T YOU WANT TO BE FORGIVEN?` · `YES, BY GOD. THE SUPPORT RESUMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pardon someone who hurt you. Start small. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of someone who hurt you in a modest way: a careless word, a broken promise, a snub. Not the deepest wound, and not anyone who is still harming you. Notice what you've been holding back from them because of it. Then ask yourself the verse's question, gently. If you pray, you can ask to be able to let it go, and to be forgiven too. The bell holds the time.
Mistah. The poor relative who spread the rumor about 'A'isha, and whom Abu Bakr chose to keep supporting anyway. Today's word.
Your line: pardon, and be pardoned. Today, give back one small thing you'd been withholding from someone over an old hurt: a greeting, a reply, a kindness. Day four hundred ninety-six.

497.title: The criterion
497.hook: the book that separates right from wrong (25:1)
497.howItsDone: Muslims use al-Furqan as one of the names of the Qur'an, alongside al-Kitab and adh-Dhikr, and teachers cite 8:29 when speaking of the clarity that comes with mindfulness of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Bakr heard the question about Mistah, don't you want to be forgiven, and your line was pardon, and be pardoned. What small thing did you give back? Day four hundred ninety-seven, the end of the week.

A ship's compass doesn't tell you where you want to go. It doesn't make the decision. It does one thing: it shows you which way north is, so that every other choice can be measured against it. Without it, at night, in fog, all directions feel the same. Today we open Surah Al-Furqan, and its first verse gives the Qur'an a name that works a little like that. Not the book, not the reading. A name that means: the thing that tells two things apart.

Pickthall: "Blessed is He Who hath revealed unto His slave the Criterion (of right and wrong), that he may be a warner to the peoples." The Criterion is al-furqan. Its root, f-r-q, means to separate, to part, to make a distinction. Faraqa: he divided. Firqa: a group that has split off. Furqan is the thing that divides: between true and false, right and wrong, the path and the drift. Pickthall adds the words of right and wrong in brackets, to say what the criterion tells apart. And the word isn't used only for this book. The Qur'an says Musa and Harun were given al-furqan too. It calls the day of the battle of Badr yawm al-furqan, the day of distinction, when two sides met and the difference between them became plain. And in Surah Al-Anfal there's a promise: if you are mindful of God, He will give you a furqan. That one is inside a person. A sense of the difference, sharpened by taqwa, that helps you see which way to go when the options blur. Tradition gives 'Umar ibn al-Khattab the title al-Faruq, the one who distinguishes, for how clearly he drew that line. So furqan works on three levels: a book, a day, and a faculty inside you. This week was full of differences: light and dark, the rumor and the good assumption, the first look and the second, walking in and knocking, the oath and the pardon. Furqan is the name for the thing that tells them apart.
screen: `AL-FURQAN: THE CRITERION.` · `F-R-Q: TO SEPARATE, TO PART.` · `MUSA, AND THE DAY OF BADR.` · `A FURQAN INSIDE YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make one clear decision. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one choice you've been leaving fuzzy. A reply you keep putting off, a habit you half-want to drop, a yes you mean as a no. Hold the two options side by side. Ask which one you'd be glad, a year from now, to have chosen. Let the difference become plain. If you pray, you can ask for a furqan. The bell holds the time.
Furqan. The criterion, the thing that tells right from wrong: a name for the Qur'an, for the day of Badr, and for a clarity inside a mindful person. Today's word.
Your line: tell right from wrong. Today, make the decision you just held, and act on it before the evening. Day four hundred ninety-seven.

myth: al-Furqan is used in the Qur'an only for the Qur'an itself
it is also used for what Musa and Harun were given, and for the day of Badr.
Pickthall adds 'of right and wrong' in brackets
to show what the criterion distinguishes.
the Qur'an promises a furqan to those who are mindful of God
Surah Al-Anfal says so: an inner sense of the difference.

fork.setup: two choices look the same in the fog. you have the Qur'an's furqan to help. what does it do?
options: it makes the decision for you.
it shows the difference, so you can choose.
it tells you to wait until the fog clears.
fork.reveal: a furqan separates: like a compass, it doesn't steer the ship, it shows which way is which.

original.note: Arabic: furqan, criterion; from the root f-r-q, to separate.

trapdoor: what you thought: another name for the Qur'an.
what it means: the thing that separates right from wrong: a book, a decisive day, and a clarity inside a mindful person.
what a scholar hears: furqan in 25:1, 2:53, 21:48 (Musa and Harun), 8:41 (Badr) and 8:29 (to the mindful); some scholars link the form to Aramaic purqan, deliverance.
